Cross section with conceptual isotherm lines in San Juan, Puerto Rico, crossing the University of Puerto Rico Río Piedras Campus (red triangle) One of the key wellbores in the hydrogeologic investigation within the SJMA was the drilling of test hole NC-3 in 1986 located on the UPR-RP campus (Figure 5a, Figure 12). This well reached a depth of 375 feet (114.3 m) and encountered, from top to bottom, surficial Quaternary deposits, the Cibao Formation, the Mucarabones Sand, and undifferentiated volcanic basement rocks of early Tertiary or Late Cretaceous age (Rodríguez-Martínez et al. 1991). The Cibao Formation displayed significant heterogeneity, including packstones, claystones, and quartz-rich sandstones with fossiliferous components (Rodríguez-Martínez et al. 1991). The Mucarabones Sand, consisting of conglomeratic quartz sandstone and claystone, reflects the fluvial-deltaic sedimentation that once dominated this area during the early Miocene (Monroe 1980; Scharlach 1990). Seven artesian zones were identified within NC-3, located across the surficial deposits, Cibao Formation, and Mucarabones Sand, producing brackish water with specific conductance between 610 and 900 microsiemens per centimeter. Yields ranged from 20 to 90 gallons per minute (GPM), with the most productive intervals in the mid-depth Cibao Formation (Rodríguez-Martínez et al. 1991). The measured water temperature in the well was 76°F (24.5°C). These results emphasize the hydrogeologic importance of the Mucarabones Sand and Cibao Formation as confined, artesian aquifers in the structurally uplifted eastern portion of the North Coast basin. 19 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. (1991) During the development of the conceptual geothermal model, several data gaps were identified that limit the accuracy and reliability of the assessment. Most notably, there is a lack of local hydraulic properties of the lower aquifer and deeper (>500 m) such as permeability, porosity, and transmissivity along with groundwater flow rate data. Islandic deep subsurface studies (Wilmarth et al. 2017) indicate that although tropical oceans exhibit warm surface temperatures, the global thermocline declines steeply beneath the shallow epipelagic zone, reaching <10°C at approximately 500 m depth and <5°C by 1,000 m. Consequently, an effectively limitless reservoir of very cold, highly permeable seawater can envelop the submerged volcanic edifices of deep-sea islands and extend beneath the freshwater lens onshore. Addressing these data gaps with advanced exploration campaigns would be essential for refining the model and increasing confidence in future analyses and decision-making. 20 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3 Infrastructure Analysis 3.1 Data Compilation – Surface The surface
